title: Cache-line-granular hot packing across cold pages
idea: A CXL controller tracks access bits per 64 B line within hot pages. It migrates the cold lines of hot pages to a compressed far tier and packs hot lines from many pages into dense hot frames through an indirection table. Tiering shifts from the 4 KB page scale to the 64 B line scale.
why: Only 20-40% of the lines in a typical hot page are hot. This needs 1.5-2x less fast DRAM for the same miss rate.

title: AMD HSA, fixed: kill shadow copies with shared virtual memory
idea: AMD's HSA/hUMA promised CPU-GPU shared pointers but died from a weak software ecosystem. Inference stacks today keep a host pinned copy, a framework copy and a GPU copy of weights; enforce single-copy with HSA-style shared page tables where the GPU maps host LPDDR directly and loaders mmap checkpoints instead of reading them into buffers.
why: Removes 2-3 redundant copies of multi-GB models in host DRAM: ~30-60% less host DRAM per inference node.

title: Fluorine-free mature-node fab builds page-compression co-processors
idea: Box: new hardware × 180 nm-class CMOS × 4 KB page compressor × fab route × i-line DNQ/novolac resist, photo-definable BCB dielectric, Cl2/HBr/BCl3 etch, O2/Cl2 chamber clean, H2-bake oxide removal, hot-phosphoric nitride strip. Vias are defined lithographically in photo-BCB rather than etched in oxide, so no CF4/C4F8/NF3/SF6, HF or PFAS photoacid is used, and the chips act as PCIe zswap accelerators.
why: Shows memory-saving silicon can be built under a full PFAS ban on a low-capital line; arrays of these compress cold pages ~2.5–3×, freeing 15–25% of host DRAM.

title: Teletext data carousel: broadcast weights to accelerators that store nothing
idea: Borrowed from broadcast TV data carousels that loop content for any receiver to catch: a rack-level weight server streams the model layer by layer in a continuous optical multicast loop from ROM/NAND, and every accelerator computes on each layer as it passes, aligning its batches to the carousel phase.
why: N accelerators share one non-volatile copy of weights with zero weight DRAM and zero refresh; per-accelerator DRAM shrinks to KV only.

title: Repurpose automotive embedded-PCM lines as U.S. weight-memory chiplets
idea: Ge-rich GST embedded PCM, whose crystallization temperature has been raised for 150 C automotive MCUs at 28/18 nm, is sold as stand-alone read-mostly weight chiplets. They are built on underused mature-node lines without EUV and hybrid-bonded under NPUs, and DRAM is reserved for activations and KV.
why: Moves read-mostly bits off scarce DRAM onto mature, U.S.-capable capacity, at far lower capital per bit than a DRAM fab (fact 4).

title: ICL DAP bit-plane storage with early-terminating dot products
idea: Store weights and keys as bit planes like the ICL Distributed Array Processor, MSB plane first, and compute dot products plane by plane, stopping as soon as the running bound proves an output's sign or top-k membership. Low-order planes are fetched only for close calls and live in a cheap slow tier.
why: On average 3-4 of 8 planes are needed, so 2-4x less HBM traffic, and only high planes need premium DRAM.

title: Magnify dedup scope to the whole rack's CXL pool
idea: Magnify deduplication from one host to a whole rack: the CXL pool controller hashes every 4 KB page and 256 B chunk from all attached hosts and keeps identical content (OS images, libraries, shared model weights, zero pages) once, as copy-on-write. The hash index sits in the switch ASIC, so hosts see ordinary loads.
why: Cloud racks run hundreds of near-identical guests. Rack-scope dedup recovers ~1.3-3x more capacity than per-host KSM, at almost no CPU cost.

title: Swap per-parameter Adam moments for count-sketch shared moment tables
idea: Substitute one moment slot per parameter with a hashed count-sketch about 1/10 the size: each parameter maps to several buckets, the median is taken on read, and exact moments are kept only for heavily updated embedding rows. Optimizer code only.
why: Adam state is 2x fp32 per parameter, often larger than the weights themselves. A sketch cuts optimizer HBM/DRAM 5-10x, so a model trains on fewer GPUs' worth of memory.

title: Day-old bakery pricing: discounted refresh-free 'ephemeral RAM' cloud tier
idea: Borrowed from bakeries selling day-old bread at a discount: a cloud instance class offers memory guaranteed only ~1 s without access (hardware refresh off), surfaced through a 'spoiled page' signal like SIGBUS; stream processors, inference servers and caches opt in at ~40% lower price per GB.
why: Creates a market that funds refresh-free hardware and moves ephemeral workloads off full-spec DRAM; dies that fail the 64 ms bin become sellable, raising effective supply.

title: Retrofit latent KV into existing models via SVD and brief finetune
idea: IFR: each token's KV is a few dozen numbers. Closest without new silicon: factor each layer's K/V projections by SVD into a shared low-rank latent (MLA-style), cache only the latent, absorb the up-projection into the query and output matrices, then heal with a short distillation finetune.
why: 4-8x KV reduction on already-trained MHA/GQA models without full retraining.

title: Kanerva sparse distributed memory replaces per-token KV slots
idea: Instead of one slot per token, keys are written into a fixed set of hard locations activated within a Hamming radius and values are superposed into counters there (Kanerva's cerebellum-inspired SDM); retrieval reads the activated locations, so memory grows with information content, not sequence length.
why: Long-context KV: a fixed 64 MB memory serving million-token contexts approximately.

title: Lighthouse beam: SiN photonic broadcast streams weights to accelerators
idea: One lighthouse serves many ships: a single weight memory broadcasts each layer over PECVD silicon-nitride waveguides (<=400 C) on a panel interposer to N accelerators at once using WDM, so each accelerator holds only a two-layer ring buffer instead of a full replica.
why: Replicas stop duplicating weights; weight DRAM per accelerator falls N-fold (8-32x).

title: DRAM-free enterprise SSDs via learned flash translation layers
idea: Imposed limit: an SSD may hold zero DRAM. The page-level mapping table (1 GB of DRAM per TB) is replaced by a learned piecewise-linear index of logical-to-physical runs plus a small SRAM delta log, exploiting the fact that most writes are sequential.
why: Enterprise SSDs carry ~0.1% of their capacity as DRAM; at hundreds of exabytes of NAND a year, removing it frees on the order of 1% of global DRAM bits.

title: Count-min and HyperLogLog sketches replace exact per-key stream state
idea: Box: probabilistic sketch × stream processor × per-key state × continuous × bounded-error counters. Counting, distinct and top-k operators keep fixed-size sketches with ~1% error bounds instead of exact per-key hash maps.
why: Per-key state stores reach terabytes; sketches cut them 100–1000× where approximate answers suffice; software only, no fluorinated inputs.

title: Manassas-plus: compressing CXL expander for domestic mature-node DRAM
idea: Po: America only makes yesterday's DRAM, so make yesterday's DRAM hold twice as much. A CXL Type-3 expander pairs Micron Manassas (VA) mature-node DRAM with a GlobalFoundries Malta (NY) 12LP+ controller doing inline LZ-class and zero-line compression with variable-size line mapping, assembled on U.S. EMS lines.
why: 2-3x effective capacity lets domestic older-node DRAM match imported leading-edge DIMMs on cost per usable bit, raising U.S.-only supply with no new fab.

title: Hardware base-relative 32-bit pointers in every load unit
idea: Inverts 'pointers are 64-bit absolute addresses': an ISA extension lets loads and stores take a 32-bit offset plus a per-region base register, so graphs, trees and object heaps store half-width pointers natively with no software decode cost.
why: Pointer-dense heaps shrink 25-45% (as JVM compressed oops show in software), across every language.

title: MRAM commit buffer: dirty pages leave DRAM the instant they are written
idea: Po: dirty pages are already safe. An Everspin (Chandler, AZ) STT-MRAM persistent write buffer on a domestic CXL card acknowledges database commits and redo records at byte granularity, so OLTP buffer pools no longer pin dirty pages or double-buffer log data while waiting for flush.
why: Write-heavy databases oversize buffer pools ~30-50% to absorb dirty pages and log buffers; persistent commit lets that DRAM shrink.

title: Retired DDR4 DIMMs pooled behind a compressing CXL controller
idea: Combine decommissioned DDR4 modules (built on pre-EUV nodes) with a 28 nm CXL pooling controller that adds inline compression and per-DIMM health remapping, deployed as the far-memory tier of new servers instead of being shredded.
why: Adds usable supply from bits that already exist with no fab; compression offsets lower density, and recyclers or OEMs can run it as a takeback business.

title: Second-life DRAM: retired DDR4 reborn in CXL cold tiers
idea: Like EV batteries repurposed for grid storage, harvest DDR4 DIMMs from decommissioned servers, bin them with a test robot, and mount them in CXL expansion boxes acting as a compressed cold tier behind new DDR5.
why: Avoids buying new bits for the coldest 30-50% of memory; supply relief at near-zero marginal cost and zero new wafers.

title: Recycled DIMM memory reefs behind CXL bridges
idea: Worsen: shred millions of retired DDR3/DDR4 DIMMs every year. Flip: test, bin and mount retired DIMMs on CXL expander boards with per-DIMM ECC and redundant spares, creating a pooled far-memory tier priced near e-waste value.
why: Cost: hardware at about $0.05-0.2/GB (bridge plus labor) vs new DRAM at $10+/GB, roughly 50-200x; trades power, bandwidth and floor space.

title: Coulomb-blockade charge packets store 3-bit KV and compute attention
idea: Store each KV element as an integer number of electrons (0-7) on silicon nanodots, where the Coulomb staircase quantizes charge natively. A key column's packets are merged onto a shared island and a single-electron transistor counts the electrons, giving the attention dot product. Physics enforces 3-bit quantization, so no codec is needed.
why: Shrinks the KV cache ~5x versus FP16, and scores never leave the array (facts 5, 8). Speculative: room-temperature blockade needs dots under 3 nm.

title: Minify weight replicas: one copy per rack, optically broadcast
idea: Minify the full weight replica each GPU node holds to one copy per rack: weights live once in a pooled memory appliance and are broadcast layer by layer over an optical memory fabric to 72 accelerators in lockstep.
why: Aggregate weight DRAM falls 9-72x, so HBM can go almost entirely to KV and activations.

title: Chloride inhibition: predictor blocks silent neurons, only active rows fetched
idea: Chloride channels stop neurons from firing; a tiny SRAM-resident low-rank predictor per FFN layer guesses which 5-10% of neurons will be non-zero for the current token, so only those weight rows are fetched from DRAM, and rarely active neurons live in flash.
why: FFN weights are about two-thirds of parameters; fetching 5-10% of rows gives ~10x fewer weight bits per token (about 10x lower energy per access), and cold neurons in flash cut weight DRAM 2-3x (energy, density).

title: Eliminate serverless warm pools with lazy snapshot-restored microVMs
idea: Idle function microVMs are snapshotted to NVMe; on invocation a userfaultfd handler restores pages lazily, prefetching a recorded working-set trace, to reach under 10 ms cold starts without keeping instances in RAM.
why: Warm pools keep 5-10x more instances resident than are executing; eliminating them cuts serverless DRAM by that factor.

title: Tattletale chip: domestic per-page access counters for exact tiering
idea: Po: memory that tattles on itself. A small GlobalFoundries Malta-fabbed companion chip on each CXL memory module counts activations per page (and per line in hot pages) from the command stream and publishes heatmaps, replacing the CPU's imprecise page-table scanning.
why: Exact hotness lets the fast DRAM tier be sized to the true hot set (often 20-40% of footprint) and doubles as row-hammer telemetry (fact 9).

title: Eliminate time-zone idle DRAM with follow-the-sun memory scheduling
idea: A global scheduler moves memory-heavy batch, training and offline-inference jobs across continents so each region's DRAM serves its local daytime peak and other regions' night-time batch load.
why: Fleet-average DRAM utilization rises from ~40% to ~70%, meaning 30-40% less DRAM must be bought for the same work.

title: Idle containers hibernate to NVMe and restore pages lazily
idea: Box: evict whole process × orchestrator × container × idle >N s × checkpoint image + userfaultfd lazy page-in. Idle services are checkpointed to local flash and their memory freed; a request wakes them in milliseconds with pages faulted in on demand.
why: 30–50% of containers are idle at any moment; reclaiming their RSS cuts node DRAM 15–30% with software only and no fluorinated inputs.

title: Pawn shop: internal market where idle gigabytes are pledged
idea: Tenants pawn idle memory: a broker daemon pays credits for GB released through a balloon driver, guarantees redemption within 50 ms from a compressed/CXL reserve, and clears prices by auction every minute so memory flows to the highest-value job.
why: Prices reveal and recover idle allocations (often 30-50%); 15-25% fewer DIMMs per fleet and a direct lever during the 4x price spike.

title: Sell retention-reject DRAM dies as ephemeral-data memory
idea: Imposed limit: no die leaves the fab as scrap. Dies that fail 64 ms retention but hold data for 1-10 ms are binned into 'ephemeral' modules reserved for short-lived data (activations, packet buffers, single-shot KV) whose lifetime software guarantees to be shorter than the measured retention.
why: Recovers a few percent of scrapped dies as usable bits from existing wafers with zero capex, and these modules need little or no refresh.

title: Mitochondrial fusion merges two half-good modules into one
idea: Damaged mitochondria fuse to complement each other's defects; the controller interleaves the healthy banks of two partially failed modules into one full-capacity logical rank via a per-bank map, so modules with dead banks are combined rather than scrapped.
why: Repair: recovers 5-15% more usable bits from fleet failures.

title: Ride-hail surge pricing for an intra-cluster DRAM spot market
idea: Borrowed from surge pricing: the cluster scheduler publishes a real-time internal price per GB-second of DRAM per rack; frameworks (Spark, LLM servers, JVMs) subscribe and automatically switch to compressed formats, smaller caches or quantized KV when the price spikes, with costs charged to team budgets.
why: Exposes DRAM scarcity to software that treats it as free; fleets that price scarce resources typically cut demand 15-30%.

title: Vision token-merging applied to KV cache compaction
idea: Combine ViT bipartite token merging with KV eviction: adjacent tokens whose keys are highly similar merge into a weighted centroid K/V with a stored count, and attention adds log(count) to the logit so merged entries keep their probability mass.
why: 2-4x KV reduction with lower quality loss than hard eviction.

title: Controller dictionary stores the 4,096 commonest lines as 12-bit handles
idea: Box: dictionary dedup × memory controller × 64 B line × on write × epoch-learned value table. The controller keeps a hardware dictionary of frequent full-line values (zeros, fill patterns, padding, one-hot rows) and stores matching lines as 12-bit handles in compact pages, refreshing the dictionary at epoch boundaries.
why: Zero and pattern lines are 10–30% of memory in many workloads; holding them at 12 bits per line gives 1.15–1.4× capacity for a few mm² of logic.

title: Developmental genome grows weights from seeds and growth rules
idea: Each weight matrix is stored as a compact 'genome' (PRNG seeds, a small hypernetwork and low-rank corrections) that is expanded tile-by-tile into SRAM at use time, the way a genome encodes a body plan instead of every cell's coordinates; DRAM holds only the genome.
why: Weight capacity: 10-50x smaller resident footprint for layers that tolerate generative parameterization, trading cheap compute for scarce DRAM bits.

title: Minify backing for zeros: 64-byte sparse-backed virtual tensors
idea: Minify physical backing so only non-zero 64 B blocks of a tensor occupy DRAM: the MMU keeps a per-block occupancy bitmap, like a sparse file, and post-ReLU activations and 90%-structured-sparse weights get no frames for their zeros.
why: With trained 90% block sparsity, tensors need ~10x less DRAM and are transparent to kernels.

title: Eliminate unneeded mantissa bits with bit-plane tensor storage
idea: Tensors are laid out as separate bit planes; a profiler sets per-tensor error budgets and the planes below them are never written, while the memory controller fetches only the planes a kernel asks for.
why: Mixed workloads hold 1.5-3x more tensors per GB, with matching cuts in fetch energy.

title: Data never comes home: query predicates applied in the network path
idea: Po: the data never enters memory. Intel Agilex FPGAs (Intel 7, fabbed in Oregon/Arizona) sit in the NIC path and apply predicates, projections and decompression to incoming storage and network streams, so host DRAM buffers hold only matching rows and needed columns.
why: Scan-heavy analytics pull 10-100x more data into DRAM than queries use; near-data filtering shrinks buffer memory and bandwidth in proportion.

title: Regenerate weights from PRNG seeds in the HBM base die
idea: A trained weight block can be approximated as a few coefficients times pseudo-random basis vectors. Store, per 8x8 block, a 16-bit LFSR seed and 4 low-bit coefficients; an LFSR array in the HBM logic die regenerates the basis and the weights at read bandwidth, replacing stored bits with deterministic computation.
why: ~3-4 bits per weight effective (4-5x smaller than FP16); spare logic-die compute becomes virtual capacity.

title: Printed diffractive 4f layer convolves images in light
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a roll-to-roll embossed phase mask in the Fourier plane of a 4f lens system applies a fixed bank of convolution kernels to incoming camera light, so the first CNN layers' feature maps, the largest activations, form on the sensor and are never stored in DRAM.
why: Early feature maps are the biggest activation buffers in vision models, often over half of activation memory; doing the first layers optically removes them.

title: Gist tokens compress old context 100x
idea: Worsen: keep KV for every raw token of a long conversation. Flip: periodically have the model compress each 1,000-token span into about 10 learned gist tokens whose KV replaces the span, with the raw text archived on cheap storage for exact re-reads.
why: Cost: 100x less KV per archived span; trades lossy recall of fine detail.

title: OS lossy heap: applications declare error tolerance per allocation
idea: Inverts 'memory must be bit-exact': a new mmap flag (MAP_LOSSY plus an error bound) sends ML activations, image buffers and analytics sketches to a region where the memory controller applies error-bounded floating-point compression (ZFP/SZ-style) on writeback. Exactness stays the default; lossy bytes are opt-in and typed.
why: 3-8x effective capacity on tolerant data, which is often 30-60% of an ML or media server's footprint.

title: Push queries into computational SSDs so buffer pools shrink
idea: Inverts 'a database must cache pages in DRAM to be fast': filters, projections and aggregations run inside SSD controllers next to the flash, so only qualifying rows reach host memory and the buffer pool is sized for results instead of the working set.
why: Analytical databases give 50-80% of server DRAM to buffer pools; pushdown can shrink that 3-10x for scan-heavy work.

title: Iodine clock reaction: hold requests, then serve whole rows at once
idea: In the iodine clock reaction nothing happens until a threshold, then everything at once; the controller holds latency-tolerant reads (prefetches, bulk KV, GC, DMA) for up to ~2 us in per-row bins and issues one activation when a bin holds 16+ requests or times out, pooling requests across all tenants sharing the device.
why: Sharing one activate/precharge across 16+ accesses cuts activation energy per access ~10x or more and raises effective bandwidth, so systems that buy DRAM channels for bandwidth (HBM especially) need fewer stacks (energy, capital).

title: 100:1 memory overcommit backed by compressed flash
idea: Worsen: give each tenant dedicated DRAM sized for its peak. Flip: overcommit physical DRAM 100:1 across bursty tenants (functions, dev environments, idle VMs) with zstd-compressed NVMe swap and working-set snapshots that restore in about 5 ms.
why: Cost: provisioned GB per physical GB rises 100x for low-duty-cycle tenants; trades cold-start latency.

title: Minify hash-table slack with near-memory probe engines
idea: Minify hash-table empty space: a near-memory probe engine runs cuckoo/Robin-Hood lookups at 95-97% load in a single round trip, instead of the 50-70% load software keeps for speed.
why: Hash-dominated key-value stores and caches need ~1.4-2x less DRAM for the same keys.

title: Batch blender: Hadamard-mix tensors so bit flips become diffuse noise
idea: Bulk blenders homogenize a batch so that no pocket is off-spec. Tensors are multiplied by a randomized Hadamard transform before quantization and storage, so after the fast inverse transform in the load path, one flipped value is spread at low amplitude across 256-4096 reconstructed values. The same rotation flattens outliers, which allows 3-4-bit quantization.
why: Sparse catastrophic errors become Gaussian-like noise about 1/sqrt(N) in amplitude, so 1%-BER storage costs only a small SNR penalty while the data is also quantized 4x.

title: 640K-style memory budgets enforced in CI and procurement
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: stop bloat before it ships; every service declares bytes-per-request and bytes-per-session budgets that CI heap profilers check (a regression fails the build), and public procurement scores bids on measured DRAM per transaction, much as 1990s developers lived within 640 KB.
why: Software memory bloat grows demand ~20%/yr; budgets need zero new silicon and could cut fleet demand growth by about a third.

title: Minify app bloat with a 'Memory Star' efficiency label
idea: Minify client DRAM demand through policy: an Energy-Star-style label rates apps by resident MB per standard task. Federal and enterprise procurement and the OS app stores require it, and OSes cap unlabeled background apps.
why: Bloated runtimes (Electron, browser tabs) use 5-10x the memory of native code. Industry-wide pressure could cut PC and phone DRAM demand ~20-40% and release supply.

title: Eliminate full fine-tune copies with 1-bit deltas over shared bases
idea: Store each fine-tuned variant as the sign of its weight delta plus per-row scales relative to one resident base model, served by a fused dequant-add GPU kernel; it is a software product.
why: Serving 100 variants needs about 1.1x base memory instead of 100x, a 10-16x saving per variant.

title: Eliminate VFIO memory pinning with IOMMU page-fault passthrough
idea: A hypervisor patch set uses ATS/PRI page-request faults so GPU/NIC passthrough VMs stop pinning all guest memory, letting those VMs be overcommitted and ballooned like ordinary ones.
why: GPU clouds strand 20-40% of host DRAM because pinned VMs cannot share; this reclaims it.

title: Direct-view storage tube revived as bistable pixels without framebuffers
idea: Tektronix direct-view storage tubes held the image on the screen with no frame memory; revive it with university-fabricated bistable pixels (ferroelectric or cholesteric liquid crystal on a glass TFT backplane) that latch their state, so phones, laptops and thin clients send only changed regions and keep no scanout framebuffer or panel self-refresh RAM.
why: Removes 50-150 MB of scanout buffers per device plus display-refresh DRAM traffic; small per device, but LPDDR is about a third of world DRAM bits, so a 1-2% cut across billions of devices frees real supply.

title: Minify the billed byte: pay-per-hot-byte cloud memory pricing
idea: Minify what customers pay for and so what clouds must provision: memory is billed by the measured hot working set (hardware access-bit sampling), and cold allocations drop automatically to a compressed/flash tier priced at 1/10.
why: Allocated memory is often 3-10x the hot set. Aligning incentives lets providers back ~10x more allocated GB with the same DRAM.

title: Typing-triggered KV rebuild: drop idle KV, recompute from tokens
idea: Reverse store-versus-recompute for cold sessions: after ~30 s idle, a session's KV is freed and only its token IDs (a few KB) are kept; when the client reports the user is typing, a compute-bound prefill rebuilds the KV on spare tensor cores before the message arrives.
why: Turns idle KV (most of chat KV) into kilobytes: 3-10x less KV memory on installed GPUs, using compute instead of new DRAM made with neon and helium.

title: Minify resident chat sessions with typing-indicator KV prefetch
idea: Minify how long an LLM session's KV cache stays in HBM/DRAM: idle sessions are parked compressed in CXL flash. A restore is triggered by early client signals (tab focus, the typing indicator, a cursor in the input box), so the ~1-3 s it takes a human to type hides the reload.
why: Most conversations sit idle >90% of wall-clock time, so the resident KV footprint drops ~3-5x with no added latency the user can see.

title: Typing-indicator-timed KV swap synchronized to user think time
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: chat traffic has a rhythm of generation followed by 10-120 s of reading and typing; page each session's KV to flash the moment generation ends and start prefetching it back when the client reports the first keystroke, hiding the swap inside human latency.
why: Turns idle-session KV, most of the resident set, into flash-resident data; 3-10x less HBM/DRAM per concurrent user.

title: Eliminate garbage-collector heap headroom with compile-time memory management
idea: Managed languages switch from tracing GC, which needs 2-5x heap headroom, to region inference plus precise reference counting with in-place reuse (Perceus-style) chosen by the compiler.
why: Heaps of Java/Go/C#-class services shrink 2-3x at equal throughput.

title: Refresh-as-scanner computing row fingerprints for free
idea: This adds zero masks. Every row is already sensed once per 32-64 ms refresh, so a tiny CRC unit at the sense-amp edge folds each refreshed row into a signature table. That gives the OS a continuously updated map of duplicate and zero rows. The DRAM's own refresh rhythm becomes the dedup scan cycle.
why: Refresh energy (46 fJ/bit, fact 3) now does useful work, and detecting duplicate and zero rows without CPU scans reclaims 10-30% of capacity.

title: 180 nm silicon-photonic links for rack-scale memory pooling
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution: replace copper memory links with optical ones built on 200 mm, 180 nm photonics lines (ring modulators and Ge photodiodes need no fine lithography), giving accelerators reach to a shared memory pool with only tens of ns of flight time, so each carries less local HBM.
why: Copper reach limits force per-device HBM; pooling cuts provisioned capacity 20-40% and the number of HBM stacks.

title: Single-copy capability fabric across kernel, driver and framework
idea: In an AI or analytics pipeline, data often sits in 3-5 copies (page cache, user buffer, framework tensor, pinned staging, device memory). Make physical frames capability-owned: storage DMA lands once in a CXL-shared frame, and ownership moves by updating a page-table capability enforced by the IOMMU instead of by memcpy.
why: 2-3x smaller host memory footprint in data loaders and serving stacks, plus less copy energy.

title: Hashing-trick embedding tables at 1% size
idea: Worsen: keep a dedicated row for every user and item ID in TB-scale embedding tables. Flip: hash IDs into a table 100x smaller with multiple hash functions and train with collisions, adding a tiny per-ID sign or scale to separate colliding IDs.
why: Cost: 100x less DRAM for recommendation embeddings; trades small accuracy loss.

title: Fused-silica volume holograms hold cold MoE experts
idea: In a large MoE most experts are idle most of the time, yet they occupy HBM. Store them as page-oriented volume holograms in femtosecond-laser-written fused silica or photopolymer on glass, read by a fixed-angle laser array and a detector array that returns a megabit page in ~1-10 us; only experts routed for the next few tokens are staged into HBM.
why: Trillion-parameter MoE needs 3-10x less HBM because only active experts stay resident; glass media cost cents per GB and retain data with zero refresh energy.

title: Minify context to gist tokens: 30x learned compression
idea: Minify a long prompt or document context into 32-64 learned 'gist' soft tokens, produced by a small compressor model. Only the gist KV is stored and reused across turns and users.
why: 16-30x less KV per cached document, so prefix caches hold 10x+ more context in the same DRAM.

title: VoIP silence suppression: never store zero or constant lines
idea: Borrowed from VoIP, which sends a tiny comfort-noise descriptor instead of silence: the memory controller keeps a per-page bitmap of zero or single-value 64-B lines, allocates no DRAM for them and synthesizes them on read, compacting the remaining lines into a smaller frame.
why: Sparse activations, fresh allocations and padded tensors are often 20-60% zero/constant lines; that capacity and bandwidth is reclaimed.

title: Fairchild CCD memory, refit as transistor-free KV-cache shift banks
idea: 1970s CCD memories were denser than DRAM but lost on random-access latency. Attention reads every token's K and V in order each decode step, so build KV banks as CCD shift registers (no access transistor per bit, ~2-4F^2) that circulate continuously past a sense row synchronized to the decode loop.
why: Density/cost per bit for the KV cache (often >50% of inference memory): removes per-cell transistors and most row/column periphery.

title: Blind-spot filling-in regenerates lost weight blocks approximately
idea: The visual cortex fills the retina's blind spot from its surroundings; weights are stored with a tiny per-layer predictor so if a recycled chip's bank dies, its weight blocks are regenerated from neighboring blocks plus a stored residual sketch, keeping the model serving until the part is swapped.
why: Lets cheap recycled DRAM hold weights without full mirroring; ~2x less redundancy overhead.

title: Minify replicas: erasure-coded in-memory stores across the rack
idea: Minify 3x in-memory replication (Redis, caches, Spark persist) to ~1.4x using Reed-Solomon (10,4) striping across rack hosts over RDMA/CXL. Parity is computed in SmartNICs, and a lost shard is reconstructed in microseconds.
why: Replicated in-memory tiers need ~2x less DRAM with the same fault tolerance.

title: Online miss-ratio curves right-size every in-memory cache
idea: Box: right-size × every application cache × cache instance × continuous × spatially sampled miss-ratio curve. Each cache samples ~0.1% of keys to build its miss-ratio curve online, and an operator shrinks caches to the knee where the marginal MB stops buying hits.
why: Caches are sized by guesswork; MRC-driven sizing typically frees 20–50% of cache memory at equal hit rate, software only, no fluorinated inputs.

title: Cloud instances discounted by measured page compressibility
idea: This adds zero masks. The provider measures each tenant's compressibility and dedup ratio over a month, places compressible tenants on compressed-memory hosts, and passes back a discount. That creates a market incentive for compressible data layouts.
why: 1.5-2x effective capacity on participating hosts, lowering fleet DRAM demand 15-25%.

title: Guests drop their page cache so one host cache serves all
idea: Reverse double caching in virtualization: guest kernels mount files through DAX over virtio-pmem/virtiofs, so file pages come straight from the host's single page cache, and guests report free pages back at once.
why: Removes the duplicate guest-plus-host cache layers, often 20-30% of VM-host DRAM, with software on today's hypervisors and no new silicon that needs rare gases.

title: Magnify similarity: LSH near-dedup with XOR deltas
idea: Magnify dedup from exact matches to near matches: locality-sensitive sketches find pages that are >=90% similar, and each is stored as a pointer to a base page plus a compressed XOR delta. Reconstruction runs inline in the CXL expander.
why: VM and container memory is full of near-duplicates that exact dedup misses. This gains a further ~1.2-2x beyond exact dedup.

title: Advance purchase commitment for US-made glass memory tiers
idea: Federal buyers (DOE labs, DoD, GSA cloud) pre-commit to buy, for example, 500 PB over 5 years of CXL warm-tier memory built on non-silicon substrates at a target of <$1/GB, paid on delivery. This lets US glass makers and idle display lines finance conversion without silicon fab capital.
why: Removes demand risk from a substrate path that needs no EUV, no helium-intensive crystal pulling and no Spruce Pine quartz crucibles, and builds US memory supply outside the DRAM oligopoly.

title: Expert-major batching streams MoE experts from QLC
idea: Worsen: keep every expert of a trillion-parameter MoE resident in HBM. Flip: store experts on QLC flash and reorder the token queue expert-major, so each expert is read from flash once per large batch and applied to every waiting token before being discarded.
why: Cost: expert weights at $0.04/GB vs $20/GB HBM, 100x+ cheaper capacity; trades per-request latency for batch throughput.

title: Bee-brain superposition: hyperdimensional associative storage for approximate lookups
idea: From insects that store rich associations in about a million neurons: many key-value pairs are bundled into one hyperdimensional vector by binding (XOR and permutation) and superposition; lookups unbind and clean up against a small codebook, degrading gracefully instead of failing.
why: For approximate caches, feature stores and candidate sets, superposition packs 5-20 associations per slot, cutting DRAM 3-10x where exactness is not required.

title: Swap per-token old KV for a holographic superposition trace
idea: Substitute discrete per-token storage with superposition. Each distant token's key and value are bound by circular convolution (holographic reduced representations) and added into a fixed d-dimensional trace per head. Recent tokens stay exact, queries unbind the trace for approximate recall, and the model is fine-tuned to tolerate the noise.
why: Old-context memory drops from O(n*d) to O(d) per head, 100x or more at 1M tokens, which caps the KV size for very long contexts. Quality is the risk.

title: Holographic binding bundles low-priority tokens into superposed vectors
idea: Peripheral KV pairs are bound by circular convolution (holographic reduced representations, akin to distributed cortical traces) and summed into a few bundle vectors per block; queries unbind to recover approximate values, cleaned up against a small codebook.
why: KV capacity: 8-16x compression on the long tail of context.

title: Diode-matrix ROM reborn as hybrid-bonded via-programmed weight layer
idea: Revive the 1950s diode-matrix ROM: frozen base-model weights are encoded by the presence and size of vias (2-3 bits per via resistance class) in a mature-node ROM wafer hybrid-bonded under the accelerator, with one programmable via mask per model. Bitlines feed straight up into the MAC arrays.
why: Capacity/cost: weights (50-80% of inference memory) leave HBM, which is then sized for KV only; via-ROM at ~2F^2 per 2-3 bits on a 28 nm wafer has no capacitor, no refresh and no EUV, roughly 5-10x lower cost per bit than DRAM.

title: Zircon fossil weights: frozen model hardwired into via-programmed ROM
idea: Zircon crystals lock elements in place for billions of years; a production 1-8B-parameter model's 4-bit weights are fossilized into via-programmed mask ROM on several accelerator dies (one via mask per model version) and read from macros next to the MAC arrays with no DRAM involved.
why: ROM reads at ~0.01-0.05 pJ/bit versus ~3-15 pJ/bit from HBM/DDR are a >100x energy-per-access cut, and weight DRAM goes to zero for that model, leaving DRAM only for KV (energy, cost/bit).

title: Eliminate sideband ECC bits for AI tensors using algorithmic checksums
idea: Put recomputable AI data on non-ECC channels and protect it with algorithm-based fault tolerance: row and column checksums on each matmul, with recompute on mismatch, so no memory ECC is needed for those regions.
why: Reclaims the 20-25% of RDIMM bits spent on ECC chips for the biggest DRAM consumer class.

title: Cross-host 64-byte line dedup inside a shared CXL pool
idea: Box: dedup × CXL pool controller × 64 B line × on write × SRAM hash index. The pool controller hashes each incoming line, keeps one physical copy with a refcount, and redirects duplicates through a two-level remap table, so dozens of hosts running the same OS, libraries and model weights share lines across machine boundaries.
why: Capacity: co-located VMs and inference replicas carry 20–50% duplicate content; pooled line dedup claims 1.3–2× effective pool capacity, i.e. 25–50% lower cost per usable bit with no new cell technology.

title: Bank-switched DIMM capacity reassigned between hosts by analog muxes
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: like EMS bank switching, a pool box of memory modules sits behind passive analog crossbar switches buildable on old processes; at millisecond-to-minute granularity a controller quiesces a module group and re-routes it from one host's channel to another's, with OS memory hot-plug onlining and offlining it.
why: Stranded DRAM is 10-25% in clouds; physical reassignment without CXL-class SerDes lets racks buy ~15% less DRAM.

title: Fiber-loop delay-line memory holds cold pages in flight
idea: Inverts 'memory is a place in space' into 'memory is time in flight': cold pages circulate in a DWDM fiber spool (10 km, 100 channels x 400 Gb/s, about 250 MB in flight per loop) with optical-electrical regeneration each lap, and a rack controller grabs a page as it passes. Average access is ~25 us, which suits far-memory tiers that today pin DRAM for cold pages.
why: Moves cold-tier bytes off DRAM onto glass and lasers, which are not supply-constrained; a wear-free swap tier that needs no DRAM wafers.

title: Eliminate peak provisioning with an internal revocable DRAM spot market
idea: A cluster agent sells revocable memory leases to batch jobs at a price set by node pressure, and reclaims leased pages within 100 ms by compressing them to zswap when the owner needs them back.
why: Raises cluster DRAM utilization from ~50% to ~80%, the equivalent of 35% more supply without new chips.

title: Count-sketch compressed Adam moments for large-model training
idea: IFR: optimizer state takes no memory. Closest without new chips: Adam's first and second moments live in a count-sketch with heavy-hitter correction; exact moments are kept only for the top 1% of parameters by gradient magnitude, the rest use sketched estimates.
why: Optimizer state is 8-12 bytes per parameter; sketching cuts training DRAM/HBM 2-3x for large models.

title: Eliminate the raw object: cache media as neural latent codes
idea: Image, video-thumbnail and document caches keep learned latent codes from a neural codec instead of raw or JPEG bytes; an inline accelerator decodes them on access, with perceptual error bounds per tenant.
why: Media-heavy in-memory caches (CDN edge, social feeds) need about 10x less DRAM.

title: Cache becomes main memory: DRAM-less servers for small-state services
idea: Reverse the hierarchy: services whose working set fits in large stacked caches (DNS, firewalls, routing, rate limiters, lookup services under ~256 MB across sockets) are rewritten to run entirely from 3D-stacked L3/SRAM with flash as backing, and their servers ship with one minimal DIMM or none.
why: Removes tens to hundreds of GB of DRAM per such node using CPU SKUs already in production, so no new DRAM bits and no rare-gas fab demand.

title: Lifetime-predicted arenas: allocate objects by when they will die
idea: Po: garbage never exists. A learned model predicts each allocation's lifetime from its call-stack signature and places objects with similar death times in the same huge-page arena, which is released whole, so fragmentation holes never form.
why: Fragmentation and huge-page bloat waste 10-30% of server heaps; lifetime grouping recovers most of it.

title: Silver-nanowire mesh reservoir holds recurrent state physically
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a roll-to-roll coated random silver-nanowire network with memristive junctions acts as a physical reservoir computer: time-series inputs drive its electrodes, the decaying junction states hold the recent history, and only a small linear readout is trained. No recurrent state or history window sits in DRAM.
why: Edge time-series models (vibration, keyword audio, ECG) buffer windows of history; a physical reservoir removes that buffer and most of the weights, bringing DRAM near zero for those tasks.

title: Widrow memistor: electroplated analog weights trained in place
idea: Revive Widrow's 1960 memistor, a resistor whose conductance was set by electroplating copper: micro-fabricated three-terminal cells with a solid electrolyte set conductance by gate current, so one analog crossbar both stores and updates weights during training.
why: Training keeps weights, gradients and Adam states (~16 bytes/param) in DRAM; in-place analog update removes most of that, a 5-10x memory cut for on-device learning.

title: Airline fare classes and overbooking for server DRAM
idea: Borrowed from airline revenue management: the hypervisor sells each host's DRAM in fare classes (guaranteed, flexible, standby) and overbooks by a learned 'no-show' rate of allocated-but-untouched pages; bumped tenants are migrated to a compressed/CXL tier and credited automatically. An EMSR-style booking-limit algorithm resets per-class caps hourly.
why: Fleet DRAM is often 30-50% allocated-but-idle; yield management turns that slack into 1.3-1.6x sellable capacity without new wafers.

title: Scatter-hoarding stashes intermediates in idle SRAM, recomputes lost ones
idea: Squirrels scatter caches widely and tolerate losing some; the runtime scatters short-lived activations across idle SRAM and register files of neighboring accelerators over the fabric, accepts eviction without notice, and recomputes lost items from cheap upstream checkpoints.
why: HBM capacity: 15-30% less DRAM for activations by harvesting stranded SRAM across a pod.

title: Minify GC heap headroom with a hardware collector
idea: Minify the 2-3x heap headroom that Java, Go and JS runtimes need for throughput. A memory-side co-processor in the controller does concurrent mark and compaction using read barriers in hardware, so heaps run at 1.1-1.2x live size without GC thrash.
why: Managed-language fleets are a large share of server DRAM. Tighter heaps cut that DRAM ~1.5-2.5x for those services.

title: Optimizer states superposed inside count-sketch arrays
idea: Inverts 'each memory cell stores exactly one value': Adam moments for huge embedding and expert tables live in a few count-sketch arrays where many parameters share cells through signed hashes, and the median of the hashed reads recovers each parameter's moment.
why: Optimizer state, normally 2-3x the weight size, shrinks 5-20x for sparse or embedding-heavy models.

title: Eliminate Adam optimizer state with moment-free sign updates
idea: Train with a sign-based optimizer whose only per-parameter state is a 1-bit error-feedback residual, removing the two fp32 moment tensors that Adam keeps for every weight.
why: Optimizer state is about 2/3 of mixed-precision training memory beyond weights; removing it cuts total training memory 40-60%.

title: Resident key sketches, full KV parked in flash
idea: Flip which part of attention lives in DRAM: only 1-bit sign sketches of the keys plus a graph ANN index stay resident, while full-precision K/V blocks live on NVMe; each decode step fetches only the top-k blocks the sketch picks.
why: Million-token contexts fit in ~1/16-1/32 of the KV DRAM, with the bulk on flash at ~10x lower cost per bit.
